title: Bring Back the Doctors

Idaho's abortion-ban referendum organizers have made a move that's almost too obvious once someone says it out loud: they've stopped arguing about abortion. The pitch now is "bring back the doctors" — because that's what actually happened when the ban went in. OB-GYNs left, and now women in a deep-red state can't get treated for a miscarriage, let alone anything more complicated. It's the gap I keep circling back to: a law gets passed to make a moral point, and eighteen months later the thing that actually shows up in people's lives is a maternity ward with no one on staff. Voters who'd never sign onto "abortion rights" might sign onto "my hospital used to have a labor and delivery unit."

Meanwhile in Iowa, Ashley Hinson is doing her own quiet subtraction — not breaking with Trump, just not standing next to him, betting her Senate race on distance rather than defiance. A Florida congresswoman did the same thing today on immigration. Neither move is bold. Both are legible: if the top of the ticket is dragging you down in the polls, you find the one issue where you can be visibly not-him and hope nobody checks the rest of your record. It's the same arithmetic every vulnerable incumbent has been running all month, except now early voting is actually underway instead of hypothetical.

And civil rights groups filed suit today to keep armed agents away from polling places — Denver's worry from a week and a half ago, grown up into an actual Voting Rights Act claim. Watching a hunch become a lawsuit is its own small, specific pleasure.
